speaking.text: A lichen is not a plant but a partnership, and for a century it was the standard textbook example of two organisms living as one. Recent genetic work has complicated that picture considerably, revealing a third partner present in most species, which had been overlooked because nobody thought to look for it.

Equal temperament divides the octave into twelve identical steps, which means that almost every interval on a piano is very slightly out of tune. Musicians accepted this compromise because it allows a single instrument to play in any key, a freedom that earlier tuning systems could not offer.

Paper money was in circulation in China some six hundred years before it appeared in Europe. The innovation arose from a practical difficulty: copper coins were heavy, and merchants trading over long distances preferred to deposit them and carry a receipt, which gradually became a currency in its own right.

Sea turtles return to the beach where they hatched after decades at sea, and they appear to do it by reading the earth's magnetic field. Each stretch of coast has a slightly different magnetic signature, and a hatchling seems to record the one it was born under before swimming away.

The Gregorian calendar reform removed ten days from October 1582, and several countries refused to adopt it for well over a century. The objection was rarely astronomical. Accepting a papal calendar carried political meaning, and Britain continued to begin its year in March until 1752.

The barcode was patented two decades before any shop could use it, because reading one required a laser cheap enough to sit at every checkout. The idea was sound and simply waited for a component, which is the ordinary history of most technologies that are later described as sudden.

lecture.transcript: I want to talk about the periodic table, and specifically about why Mendeleev is credited with it when at least five other people proposed something similar within the same decade. Several of them arranged the elements by atomic weight and noticed the repeating pattern of properties. Newlands in England published his law of octaves in 1865 and was mocked at a meeting of the Chemical Society, where somebody asked whether he had tried arranging them alphabetically. So priority is genuinely contested. What distinguishes Mendeleev is not the arrangement but what he was willing to do with it. When an element did not fit, he left a gap rather than forcing it, and then he did the thing that made his reputation: he described the missing elements in detail. He specified atomic weight, density, colour, the formula of the oxide, even how the substance would behave when heated. He named three of them provisionally after their neighbours. Within fifteen years all three had been discovered, and the measured properties matched his predictions closely enough that the agreement could not be coincidence. Now, the point I want to draw out is about what makes a classification scientific rather than merely tidy. Any arrangement of data can look meaningful in retrospect. Mendeleev's was falsifiable in advance, because he had committed himself to statements that could have been shown wrong by a single measurement, and it is that exposure to refutation rather than the neatness of the grid that made the table more than a filing system.
key: at least five others proposed similar arrangements in the same decade, and Newlands was mocked for his
what distinguished Mendeleev was leaving gaps rather than forcing elements to fit

all three predicted elements were found within fifteen years and matched closely

lecture.transcript: Architectural acoustics became a science almost by accident, and the story is worth telling because of how the problem was framed. In 1895 Harvard opened a lecture theatre in which speech was unintelligible. Sound persisted so long that each syllable overlapped the next, and the building was unusable for its purpose. A young physicist called Wallace Sabine was asked to fix it, with no theory to work from, because nobody had ever quantified how sound decays in a room. What Sabine did was almost absurdly laborious. He worked at night when the building was quiet, borrowed seat cushions from a nearby theatre, and measured by ear, using an organ pipe and a stopwatch, how long a sound remained audible after the source stopped. Then he added cushions, one batch at a time, and measured again. Hundreds of nights of this produced a simple relationship: reverberation time is proportional to the volume of the room and inversely proportional to the total absorption in it. That single equation turned acoustics from a matter of intuition into something you could calculate before building. And here is the part I find instructive. Sabine did not discover a new physical principle. Everything in his equation was already understood. What he supplied was a measurement procedure for a quantity nobody had thought to measure, and that is frequently what a new field actually consists of.

Sabine had no existing theory of how sound decays in rooms

swt.passage: Garrett Hardin's essay on the tragedy of the commons is among the most cited papers in the social sciences, and its central claim has been substantially overturned by the researcher who examined it most carefully. Hardin argued that any resource held in common will inevitably be destroyed, because each user gains the full benefit of taking more while bearing only a fraction of the cost. The logic is compelling and the conclusion, that commons must be either privatised or placed under state control, was adopted widely in development policy. Elinor Ostrom's objection was empirical rather than theoretical. She and her collaborators documented hundreds of commons, some managed continuously for centuries, in which communities had devised rules that prevented exactly the collapse Hardin described. Swiss alpine pastures, Japanese village forests and Spanish irrigation systems all fell into this category. What Hardin had described was not a commons but an open-access resource with no governance at all, a situation that is real but far from universal. Ostrom's further contribution was to identify what the successful systems shared: clear boundaries, rules adapted to local conditions, cheap conflict resolution, and users who participated in making the rules that bound them. Her work earned a Nobel Prize and has been rather less widely absorbed than the essay it corrected.
key: Hardin argued commonly held resources are inevitably destroyed by individual incentives
his conclusion favoured privatisation or state control and shaped development policy
Ostrom documented hundreds of commons managed sustainably for centuries

swt.passage: The index is a medieval invention that changed how books are read, and its arrival marks a shift from reading as a linear discipline to reading as retrieval. Before the thirteenth century a scholar approached a text from the beginning, and knowledge of where a passage sat depended entirely on memory, which was trained deliberately and to a degree now hard to imagine. The alphabetical index arose in the universities and preaching orders, where a friar preparing a sermon needed to locate every scriptural reference to a particular theme quickly, and had no time to read an entire volume to find them. Constructing one required an ordering principle that contemporaries found faintly disreputable, since alphabetical order deliberately ignores the logical or theological relationships between subjects and treats them as arbitrary. Several writers objected that this trained the mind to grasp fragments rather than wholes, an argument reproduced almost word for word in modern complaints about search engines. What the index actually accomplished was to make large books usable by people who had not memorised them, and in doing so it changed what a book could be: not a text to be absorbed entire, but a resource to be consulted.
key: before the index, reading was linear and depended on trained memory
the alphabetical index arose in universities and preaching orders for rapid retrieval
alphabetical order was distrusted because it ignores logical relationships between subjects
contemporaries argued it trained the mind to grasp fragments, an argument echoed about search engines
the index made large books usable without memorising them and turned a book into a resource to consult

reading.passage: The wisdom of crowds is real but conditional, and the conditions are routinely ignored by people invoking it. The classic demonstration involves a large number of independent guesses about a quantity, whose average proves more accurate than almost any individual estimate. The mechanism is straightforward: errors in opposite directions cancel, provided they are genuinely independent. That proviso does most of the work. When participants can see one another's answers, independence collapses, estimates converge, and the group becomes confident and wrong at the same time. Experiments in which guessers were shown the running average produced tighter clustering and worse accuracy than experiments in which they were kept apart. The practical implication runs against ordinary intuition about meetings: a group that discusses a question before estimating it will typically do worse than the same group estimating privately first and discussing afterwards. Aggregation is powerful, but it is aggregation of independent judgements, and a discussion is precisely the mechanism that destroys the independence it depends on.

Estimating privately before discussion is likely to outperform discussing first.

reading.passage: Gamification, the practice of adding points, badges and leaderboards to activities that are not games, has produced results that are strong in the short term and unreliable afterwards. The reliable finding is that extrinsic rewards increase the rewarded behaviour while they are present. The less convenient finding is what happens when they are withdrawn: participants frequently perform below their original baseline, apparently because the reward has reframed an activity that was previously done for its own sake into work performed for payment. Designers who understand this build systems in which the points track progress toward a goal the user already had, rather than substituting for one. Those who do not tend to produce applications with excellent engagement metrics for six weeks and an abandonment rate that nobody includes in the case study.
reading.q: What does the passage identify as the central risk of gamification?
options: Rewards can displace an existing intrinsic motivation, leaving behaviour worse than before once they stop.
Points and badges have no measurable effect on behaviour at any stage.
Users find leaderboards demotivating because they encourage comparison.
Gamified systems are more expensive to build than conventional ones.

reading.passage: Broken windows policing rests on a proposition that is intuitively appealing and empirically fragile: that visible disorder signals an absence of control and thereby invites serious crime. Cities that adopted the approach in the 1990s did see crime fall, which is the evidence usually cited. The difficulty is that crime fell across almost every large city in the same period, including those that adopted no such policy and several that reduced policing levels. When researchers have attempted to isolate the effect using variation in enforcement intensity between comparable neighbourhoods, the estimated impact on serious crime has been small or indistinguishable from zero, while the measurable costs, in arrests for minor offences concentrated in particular communities, have been substantial and unevenly distributed.
reading.q: What is the author's main argument?
options: The crime decline attributed to the policy occurred in cities that did not adopt it, weakening the causal claim.
Visible disorder has been proven to have no relationship with serious crime.
The policy was effective but was applied too aggressively in some cities.
Researchers have been unable to measure enforcement intensity in any neighbourhood.

listening.transcript: I want to talk about why election polling goes wrong, because the usual explanation, that people lie to pollsters, is the least important of the actual reasons. Start with the sampling problem. A poll needs a sample that resembles the electorate, and getting one has become extraordinarily difficult. Response rates to telephone polls have fallen from around thirty-six per cent in the late nineteen nineties to under six per cent now. That does not automatically bias the result, but it means the people who do answer differ from those who do not in ways the pollster has to guess at and correct for. Those corrections are called weighting, and they are where most of the trouble lives. If you weight by age, sex and region, you are assuming that within each of those categories the respondents resemble the non-respondents. Recent evidence suggests they do not: people who answer surveys are systematically more socially trusting and more politically engaged than people who do not, and no amount of demographic weighting fixes a difference on a variable you have not measured. Then there is the turnout problem, which is separate and arguably worse. A poll measures preference among people surveyed; an election measures the preference of people who actually vote. Bridging that gap requires a model of who will turn out, and turnout models are built from previous elections, which means they systematically fail in exactly the elections where turnout patterns change. And that is precisely when everyone is paying attention. What I want you to notice is that none of these are errors of arithmetic. The margin of error quoted in the newspaper describes only the sampling variation, and it is almost always the smallest of the uncertainties involved.
key: the common explanation that respondents lie is the least important reason

weighting assumes respondents resemble non-respondents within demographic categories, which evidence contradicts
survey respondents are more socially trusting and politically engaged on variables not measured

I want to deal with the claim that Napoleon was unusually short, because it is a useful example of how a piece of misinformation can be manufactured. Contemporary records give his height as five feet two inches in French units, which converts to roughly five feet six or seven in English measure, slightly above the average for a Frenchman of his generation. The confusion between the two systems accounts for part of the story. The rest is deliberate. British caricaturists, Gillray in particular, drew him as a tiny figure in oversized boots for two decades, and the image was effective propaganda precisely because it was ridiculous rather than fearsome. So the myth has two ingredients: a genuine unit conversion error, and a sustained political campaign that had every reason to encourage it.

listening.transcript: A word about laboratory notebooks, which I know feels like an administrative imposition until the first time it saves you. Write down what you actually did, not what the protocol says you should have done. If you used a different buffer because the right one had run out, that goes in the book. If the incubation ran forty minutes instead of thirty because you were called away, that goes in too. The temptation is always to record the idealised version, because the real version looks careless. But the whole value of the notebook is that when an experiment fails to replicate three months later, the difference between the two runs is sitting in the record, and it is almost always one of these small deviations that felt too trivial to mention.

options: Record what was actually done, including small deviations from the protocol.

listening.transcript: Engineers designing systems that must not fail rarely make a single component stronger. They duplicate it, and they duplicate it in a way that means the two copies will not fail for the same reason: different manufacturers, different materials, sometimes different physical principles altogether. A backup identical to the original protects against wear but not against a design flaw, so what is really being purchased is not duplication but [BEEP].

listening.spoken: An octopus can change the colour and texture of its skin in under a second yet the animal is almost certainly colour blind It has a single visual pigment, which should make discrimination between wavelengths impossible One proposed explanation is that the unusual shape of the pupil spreads different colours to different depths, so the animal could judge colour by adjusting focus rather than by comparing receptors. The skin itself also contains light-sensitive proteins which may allow it to sense its background directly.

The first reasonably accurate measurement of the speed of light came from astronomy rather than from any laboratory In 1676 Rømer noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moons ran late when the earth was furthest from Jupiter and early when it was nearest. He correctly inferred that the difference was the time light took to cross the extra distance and derived a figure within about a quarter of the modern value at a time when many astronomers still assumed light travelled instantly
